name: MACD signal-line crossover

origin.source_title: Moving Average Convergence-Divergence, introduced in Appel's newsletters in the late 1970s (date approximate)

how_it_works.simple: Take a fast average and a slow average of price and look at the gap between them. When that gap starts growing upward past its own average, buy; when it turns down past it, sell.
how_it_works.analogy: Like watching a car's speed rather than its position: you act when it starts to speed up or slow down.
how_it_works.precise: MACD is EMA(12) minus EMA(26) of price; the signal line is a 9-period EMA of MACD. The retail rule buys when MACD crosses above the signal line and sells when it crosses below; a variant (MACD(12,26,0)) trades the zero line. Chong and Ng (2008) and Chong, Ng and Liew (2014) test these on stock indices.

rule: Daily: MACD = EMA12(close) - EMA26(close); signal = EMA9(MACD). Go long when MACD crosses above the signal line, exit (or go short) when it crosses below. The academic variant MACD(12,26,0) uses the zero line instead of the signal line.
economic_rationale: It is a smoothed momentum measure, so any edge would come from short-term trend persistence. Chong, Ng and Liew (2014) say their results 'shed some light on investors' belief' in it, not that a risk premium explains it.
why_it_might_fail: Results in Chong, Ng and Liew (2014) are uneven across markets: the rule was significant in Milan and Toronto but not everywhere, which is what one would expect from chance across many market tests. The 12/26/9 parameters were never chosen with out-of-sample testing, and signal-line crossovers trade often, so costs matter.

reported_results.source: Chong, Ng and Liew (2014), Journal of Risk and Financial Management 7(1), abstract
reported_results.market: Stock indices of five OECD countries
reported_results.notes: Abstract read through its OpenAlex record (full text blocked to our fetcher). MACD(12,26,0) and RSI(21,50) 'consistently generate significant abnormal returns' in the Milan Comit General and the S&P/TSX Composite; no numbers in the abstract. Builds on Chong and Ng (2008) for the FT30 in London.

implementations.notes: Python wrapper for TA-Lib; has SMA, EMA, MACD, RSI, Bollinger bands and candlestick pattern functions.
General daily-bar backtester; its standard example is an SMA crossover.

relevance.reason: Easy to test on SPY and daily FX, but likely to behave like a noisier moving average crossover.
